theme: QUO — primary quotes read in context
checked: Sampled 44 links with a quoted primary source, 4-5 per era for eras 1-9 (era from the inventory's drafted_in; era-9 parts 1 and 2 merged as era 9, the Armenian Apostolic folder counted as era 8). Method: Python random.seed(1109); per era, links with at least one primary quote sorted by id and shuffled, then 3 Documented and 2 non-Documented taken, preferring a link type not yet picked in that era; one primary quote per link chosen with random.choice. 26 Documented, 18 other (10 Widely Accepted, 8 Inferential-Thin); all six types covered; lanes 1-8 and two bridges. Each quote read with at least 12-20 lines either side in the vendored file (more where the speaker or subject needed it), and where the sampled quote was only supporting I read the link's other primary sources too. Results: 41 clear, 3 findings from the sample (1 note clipping that reverses the source, 1 cross-era note/grade reasoning inconsistency, 1 period mismatch), plus 1 cross-era source-kind labelling inconsistency found while checking a sampled link (36 primary sources whose work field names an editor's note/introduction scanned; 4 are modern editors' own statements labelled primary). No cluster: the failures fall in eras 2, 7 and 9 and in different source files; the only other link using the Sotelo (Pagès) or Cocks file is the same link.

findings.finding: The note clips Sotelo's sentence so it says the opposite of the source. It says the 1614 ban 'sent every missionary out of Japan'. Sotelo's very next words say most of them defied the edict and stayed hidden, and that their work kept the faith alive. That is the thread that matters for a link to the hidden Christians, and the note erases it.
findings.evidence: cic/texts/pages_histoire-religion-chretienne-japon-annexes-fra_1870.txt:6913-6922: 'religiosi quoque omnes generali Imperatoris edicto relegati; plerique tamen illorum, proprias vitas, contra Impera-' [page break] '-is edictum, coniemnentes, diversis in locis occultati remanse-[ru]nt : quorum labore, doctrina et exemplo fides in multis fidelibus egerrima conservatur'. Cocks (cocks_diary-v1_thompson1883.txt:2588-2590) records the edict only, which matches 'noted the ban'.

edits.new: A Franciscan report of the 1620s says the ban of 1614 exiled every missionary from Japan. Yet most of them stayed on in hiding, it adds, and kept the faith alive. The English trader Richard Cocks noted the ban in 1615. The tie to the hidden Christians found in 1865 rests on modern studies alone, so it is thin.

findings.finding: Two 'continued as' links with the same kind of evidence, a bishop named before the split and one after, got opposite reasoning. Aksum is Documented under the era-1 bar, 'the see shown on both sides', even with a 170-year gap (era-2 review R1-02, kept in round 2). Palestine is Inferential-Thin, and its note gives the reason that 'neither traces the bishops between them'. But the same vendored Eusebius does trace them. He names Zabdas as bishop of Jerusalem after Hymenaeus, then Hermon, and says the apostolic chair 'has been preserved there until the present time'. So the note's stated reason is wrong. The real difference from Aksum is that the Palestinian movement has no continuesAs and centres on Caesarea and Origen, so it is not a clean period split into the Jerusalem pilgrimage church. Proposed: keep Inferential-Thin, add the succession lines, and have the note give the true reason.

edits.new: In the library at Aelia, as Jerusalem was then called, Eusebius saw letters that Bishop Alexander had gathered. He names the next bishops of the city down to Hermon. He says their chair was kept there until his own time. Later, Constantine wrote to Macarius, its bishop, about building the Church of the Saviour. The see carried on, but that the new pilgrim church was the same community is only an inference.

findings.finding: This Documented link rests on a single quote, from Jacobs's 1911 preface (lines 96-308 are the 1911 preface, not the first-edition one). The movement it points to is dated 1817-1906. Its text is about the Prussian Old Lutherans, the Saxon emigrants and Missouri, Erlangen and Löhe, and does not mention the General Council. So the speaker comes after the movement's end date and from a body its own text does not name. The era-9 review made this call on purpose ('the General Council belongs to the American confessional revival'), so I log it rather than overturn it.

findings.finding: The same kind of source is labelled differently across eras. A modern editor's own statement is 'secondary' in most eras: McGiffert's note in era 1, Fremantle's Rufinus introduction in era 2, Moberg's introduction in era 3, Gwynn in era 4. Four links label such statements 'primary'. Moberg's same introduction is primary on Aksum but secondary on aksumite-christianity--cyrilline. Fremantle's prolegomena and introduction are primary on two era-2 links, while his Rufinus introduction is secondary in the same era. Mirbt's 1911 note on Gul's 1892 election is labelled primary. None of the four grades rests on the relabelled source; each link keeps other true primaries.
